phy_edx.8.0.summary: Forces are interactions between two objects, and Edexcel 1PH0 sorts them into contact forces (the objects must touch, such as normal contact force, friction, air resistance, tension and upthrust) and non-contact forces (acting at a distance through a field: gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic). Every interaction produces a pair of forces, equal in size and opposite in direction, acting on the two different objects. Because forces have both size and direction they are vector quantities, so they are drawn as arrows whose length shows the magnitude and whose direction shows the way the force acts.

core.p: A **force** is a push or a pull that comes from an **interaction** between two objects. Forces can change an object's speed, direction of motion or shape. Force is measured in **newtons (N)**.
bullets: Every force needs **two objects**: the one exerting it and the one it acts on.
A force has a **size (magnitude)** and a **direction**, so it is a **vector** quantity.
Forces are shown as **arrows**: length shows size, arrowhead shows direction.
A **resultant force** changes the motion of an object (acceleration).
Forces are classified as **contact** or **non-contact** forces.

callouts.p: A push or a pull on an object caused by an interaction with another object; measured in newtons (N).

core.p: A **contact force** only acts when the objects are **physically touching**. Remove the contact and the force disappears.
bullets: **Normal contact force** (reaction force): a surface pushes back on an object pressing on it, acting at 90 degrees to the surface.
**Friction**: opposes the relative motion (or attempted motion) of two surfaces sliding over each other.
**Air resistance / drag**: a frictional force on an object moving through air or water, opposing the motion.
**Tension**: the pulling force in a stretched rope, string or cable.
**Upthrust**: the upward push of a fluid on an object partly or fully immersed in it.
**Thrust**: the forward push of an engine, e.g. on a rocket or jet.

callouts.p: A force that acts between two objects that are physically touching.

core.p: When you rest a book on a table, the book pushes down on the table. The table's particles are pushed slightly closer together and push back on the book. This upward push is the **normal contact force**.
bullets: It always acts **perpendicular (normal)** to the surface.
For an object resting on a horizontal surface, it is **equal in size** to the object's weight.
It **adjusts** to match the push on the surface, up to the point where the surface breaks.
It is a **contact** force; the weight of the book is a **non-contact** force.
Weight and normal contact force on the book are **not** an interaction pair: they act on the **same** object and are different types of force.

fig.cap: A book resting on a table. Weight (gravity, non-contact) acts down on the book; the normal contact force from the table acts up on the book. They are balanced, so the resultant force is zero.

core.p: **Friction** is a contact force that acts when two surfaces slide or try to slide over each other. It always acts **opposite** to the direction of motion (or attempted motion).
bullets: Caused by rough surfaces catching and interlocking as they move past each other.
Friction does work, transferring energy to the **thermal store** of the surfaces (they heat up).
**Useful** friction: brakes, grip of tyres on the road, walking without slipping.
**Unwanted** friction: wear and heating in engines and machinery (reduced by lubrication).
Air resistance and water resistance (**drag**) are forms of friction that increase with speed.

callouts.p: Friction does not always act backwards relative to you; it acts opposite to the motion of the surfaces relative to each other.

core.p: A **non-contact force** acts between objects that are **not touching**. It acts at a distance because each object is in the other's **field**: a region where a force is felt.
bullets: **Gravitational force**: acts between any two objects with **mass**, in a gravitational field. It is always **attractive**.
**Electrostatic force**: acts between **charged** objects in an electric (electrostatic) field. Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
**Magnetic force**: acts between magnets, or a magnet and a magnetic material (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt), in a magnetic field. Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
Non-contact forces get **weaker** as the distance between the objects increases.
They act through empty space (a vacuum), e.g. the Sun's gravity on Earth.

callouts.p: A force that acts between two objects that are not touching, because one is in the field of the other.

core.h: Weight: gravity as a non-contact force
core.p: **Weight** is the gravitational force on an object due to the Earth's gravitational field. It acts at a distance, so it is a non-contact force.
bullets: weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = m x g).
On Earth g = 10 N/kg (used on Edexcel papers).
Weight acts from the object's **centre of mass**, towards the centre of the Earth.
Weight is a force (N); mass is the amount of matter (kg).
The object also pulls the Earth upwards with an equal force.

callouts.p: A falling skydiver has weight even though nothing touches them; air resistance on them is the contact force.

core.p: Whenever two objects interact, **both** objects feel a force. These two forces form an **interaction pair** (Newton's third law).
bullets: The two forces are **equal in size**.
They act in **opposite directions**.
They act on **different objects** (one on each).
They are the **same type** of force (both gravitational, both contact, etc.).
Because they act on different objects, they **never cancel** each other out.
Example: you push on a wall; the wall pushes back on you with an equal force.

callouts.p: Same size, opposite direction, same type, on different objects.

fig.cap: A gravitational interaction pair: the Earth pulls the Moon and the Moon pulls the Earth with a force of the same size in the opposite direction, each acting on a different object.

core.h: Pairs of forces represented as vectors
core.p: Because forces have size and direction, each force in a pair can be drawn as a **vector arrow**.
bullets: Draw both arrows the **same length** (same magnitude).
Point them in **opposite directions**.
Start each arrow on the object the force acts **on**.
Label each arrow with the type of force and its size, e.g. '20 N magnetic force on magnet A'.
Use a scale (e.g. 1 cm = 10 N) when drawing to scale.

core.p: Students often confuse an interaction pair with two balanced forces on one object. They are not the same thing.
bullets: **Balanced forces** act on the **same object** and can be different types (weight and normal contact force on a book).
**Interaction pairs** act on **different objects** and are the same type.
For the book: the pair to the book's weight is the book's gravitational pull **on the Earth**.
The pair to the table's normal force on the book is the book's contact push **on the table**.

callouts.p: Weight and normal contact force on a resting book are NOT a Newton's third law pair.

core.p: Questions describe a situation and ask you to name forces and say whether they are contact or non-contact.
bullets: Car driving: thrust from road on tyres (contact), friction, air resistance (contact), weight (non-contact), normal contact force.
Skydiver: weight (non-contact), air resistance (contact).
Boat floating: weight (non-contact), upthrust (contact).
Charged balloon on wall: electrostatic attraction (non-contact).
Fridge magnet: magnetic force (non-contact), friction holding it from sliding (contact).

callouts.p: For non-contact forces, name the field: gravitational, electric (electrostatic) or magnetic. That link is in the spec.

core.p: A field is a region of space in which an object experiences a force. Objects create fields around them, and other objects placed in the field feel a force.
bullets: A **mass** creates a gravitational field; another mass in that field is attracted.
A **charge** creates an electric field; another charge in it is attracted or repelled.
A **magnet** creates a magnetic field; a magnet or magnetic material in it feels a force.
The field is **stronger closer** to the object, so the force is bigger at short distances.
This is why the Moon's gravity on you is tiny but the Earth's is large.

analogy.p: A contact force is like a handshake: two people must physically touch, and both feel the grip at the same time with the same strength. A non-contact force is like a phone call: the two people can be far apart and still affect each other through an invisible link (the field), and the signal gets weaker the further apart they are. Where it breaks down: a phone call can go one way (one person talks, the other listens), but forces always act on both objects equally, and fields need no device or wires to carry them.

terms.d: A push or pull resulting from an interaction between two objects; measured in newtons (N).
The unit of force.
A force between objects that are physically touching.
A force between objects that are not touching, acting through a field.
A region where an object experiences a force, e.g. gravitational, electric or magnetic.
The force from a surface on an object pressing on it, acting at 90 degrees to the surface.
A contact force opposing the relative motion of two surfaces in contact.
A frictional contact force on an object moving through a fluid, opposing its motion.
The pulling force in a stretched string, rope or cable.
The upward force from a fluid on an object immersed in it.
An attractive non-contact force between any two objects with mass.
The gravitational force on an object, W = m x g.
A non-contact force between charged objects; like charges repel, unlike attract.
A non-contact force between magnets or a magnet and magnetic material.
Two forces of equal size and opposite direction, of the same type, acting on two different interacting objects.
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as force.

mistakes.w: Weight is a contact force because the ground pushes on you
mistakes.r: Weight is a non-contact (gravitational) force; the ground's push is the normal contact force

mistakes.w: Weight and normal contact force on a book are an interaction pair
mistakes.r: They act on the same object; the pair to the book's weight is the book's pull on the Earth

mistakes.w: The pair of forces cancel out
mistakes.r: Interaction pair forces act on different objects so they cannot cancel

mistakes.w: Friction acts in the direction of motion
mistakes.r: Friction opposes the motion (or attempted motion)

mistakes.w: Magnetic force attracts all metals
mistakes.r: Magnetic forces act on magnetic materials: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt

mistakes.w: Gravity can repel
mistakes.r: Gravitational force is always attractive

mistakes.w: Air resistance is non-contact because air is invisible
mistakes.r: Air resistance is a contact force: air particles collide with the object

mistakes.w: Non-contact forces stay the same at any distance
mistakes.r: Non-contact forces get weaker as the distance between objects increases

mistakes.w: Electrostatic force acts between magnets
mistakes.r: Electrostatic forces act between charged objects; magnetic forces act between magnets

exam.q: Which of these is a non-contact force: friction, tension, magnetic force, upthrust?
model: Magnetic force
exam.tip: The three non-contact forces are gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic.

exam.q: State the difference between a contact force and a non-contact force.
model: Contact force: objects must be touching
Non-contact force: acts at a distance / objects not touching (through a field)
exam.tip: Give both halves.

exam.q: Name two contact forces.
model: Any two from: friction, air resistance/drag, normal contact force/reaction, tension, upthrust, thrust
exam.tip: Avoid vague answers like 'pushing'.

exam.q: Name the field involved when a charged rod attracts small pieces of paper.
model: Electric / electrostatic field
exam.tip: Charge goes with electrostatic.

exam.q: A book rests on a table. Describe the force that is paired with the weight of the book.
model: Gravitational force of the book on the Earth
same size as the book's weight
acting upwards / opposite direction
exam.tip: The pair acts on a different object and is the same type of force.

exam.q: Explain why the forces in an interaction pair do not cancel out.
model: They act on different objects
forces only cancel if they act on the same object
exam.tip: Mention 'different objects' explicitly.

exam.q: A skydiver falls through the air. Name the two forces acting on the skydiver and state whether each is a contact or non-contact force.
model: Weight
non-contact
Air resistance / drag
contact
exam.tip: One mark for each name and classification.

exam.q: Two magnets are held with north poles facing each other. Magnet A exerts a force of 0.5 N on magnet B. Describe the force that magnet B exerts on magnet A.
model: away from B / opposite direction (repulsive)
magnetic force
exam.tip: Size, direction, type.

exam.q: Describe how to represent the pair of forces between two repelling charged spheres on a diagram.
model: Two arrows of equal length, one on each sphere
pointing in opposite directions away from each other
exam.tip: Arrows start on the object the force acts on.

exam.q: Explain, with examples, how objects can interact with and without contact. Refer to the fields involved and the forces produced.
model: Contact interactions need objects to touch, e.g. normal contact force from a table on a book
Friction between sliding surfaces opposes motion
Non-contact interactions act at a distance through a field
Gravitational field: masses attract, e.g. Earth and Moon / weight
Electric field: charges, like repel and unlike attract
Magnetic field: magnets and magnetic materials, like poles repel
Each interaction gives a pair of equal and opposite forces on the two objects, shown as vector arrows
exam.tip: Cover contact, all three fields, and the force pair idea for top level.

worked.q: A boat floats on a lake while being pulled by a rope from the shore. List the forces acting on the boat and classify each.
steps: Weight of boat: gravitational, non-contact, acts downwards
Upthrust from water: contact, acts upwards
Tension in the rope: contact, acts towards the shore
Water resistance (drag): contact, opposes the motion

worked.q: The Earth pulls an apple of mass 0.2 kg with a gravitational force. Calculate this force and describe the force the apple exerts on the Earth. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: W = m x g = 0.2 x 10 = 2 N downwards on the apple
Interaction pair: the apple pulls the Earth with a gravitational force
Same size: 2 N
Opposite direction: upwards, towards the apple, acting on the Earth
worked.ans: 2 N on the apple; the apple pulls the Earth upward with 2 N (gravitational, non-contact)

worked.q: A balloon rubbed on hair sticks to a wall. Explain the forces involved.
steps: Rubbing transfers electrons, so the balloon becomes charged
The charged balloon is in an electric field interaction with the wall's charges
There is an electrostatic attraction (non-contact) between them
Where the balloon touches the wall, normal contact force and friction (contact) stop it sliding down
worked.ans: Electrostatic attraction (non-contact) holds it to the wall; friction and normal contact force (contact) act at the surface

phy_edx.8.1.summary: Every physical quantity is either a scalar or a vector. A scalar quantity has magnitude (size) only, such as distance, speed, mass, energy and time, while a vector quantity has both magnitude and a specific direction, such as displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight and momentum. Edexcel 1PH0 expects you to explain this difference using examples, to represent vectors as arrows whose length shows magnitude, and to use the idea of direction to explain things like why an object moving at constant speed in a circle has a changing velocity.

core.h: Scalars and vectors: the key difference
core.p: Physicists split quantities into two groups depending on whether **direction matters**.
bullets: A **scalar** quantity has **magnitude (size) only**.
A **vector** quantity has **magnitude and direction**.
Magnitude is the size of the quantity, always with a unit.
Direction can be given as left/right, up/down, north/east, a bearing or an angle, or a + or - sign.
Two vectors with the same size but different directions are **different** vectors.

callouts.p: A quantity that has magnitude only.
A quantity that has both magnitude and a specific direction.

core.p: Edexcel names these examples. Learn them as matching pairs where possible.
bullets: **Vectors**: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum.
**Scalars**: distance, speed, mass, energy, time.
Other scalars: temperature, power, volume, density, charge, potential difference.
Matching pairs: distance (scalar) and displacement (vector); speed (scalar) and velocity (vector); mass (scalar) and weight (vector).

callouts.p: Distance and displacement have the same unit (m). You decide scalar or vector by asking: does it have a direction?

core.p: **Distance** is how far an object travels along its path, whatever the direction. **Displacement** is the straight-line distance from start to finish **in a stated direction**.
bullets: Distance is a scalar; displacement is a vector.
Walk 4 m east then 3 m north: distance = 7 m, displacement = 5 m (at an angle north of east).
Run once round a 400 m track: distance = 400 m, displacement = 0 (back at the start).
Displacement can be zero or negative; distance cannot decrease.
Displacement magnitude is always less than or equal to the distance.

core.p: **Speed** is how fast something is moving (distance per unit time). **Velocity** is speed **in a given direction** (displacement per unit time).
bullets: speed = distance / time; velocity = displacement / time.
Both measured in **m/s**.
A car at 20 m/s north and a car at 20 m/s south have the **same speed** but **different velocities**.
Velocity changes if the speed changes **or** the direction changes.
Velocities in opposite directions can be written as + and -, e.g. +5 m/s and -5 m/s.

callouts.p: Always state a direction when giving a velocity, e.g. 15 m/s to the left.

core.h: Circular motion: constant speed, changing velocity
core.p: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is **always changing direction**, so its **velocity is changing** even though its speed is not.
bullets: The direction of motion at any instant is along the tangent to the circle.
Changing velocity means the object is **accelerating** (acceleration is a vector).
A resultant force towards the centre causes this change in direction.
Examples: a satellite in orbit, a car on a roundabout, a ball on a string.

callouts.t: Constant speed is not constant velocity
callouts.p: In a circle the speed can be constant but the velocity is changing because the direction changes.

core.p: **Mass** is the amount of matter in an object, a scalar measured in kg. **Weight** is the gravitational force on the object, a vector measured in N that acts towards the centre of the Earth.
bullets: weight = mass x gravitational field strength: W = m x g.
On Earth g = 10 N/kg, so a 5 kg mass has a weight of 50 N downwards.
Mass is the same everywhere; weight depends on the gravitational field strength.
Weight always has a direction (down, towards the centre of the planet), so it is a vector.

core.p: These are vectors because their direction affects what happens.
bullets: **Force** (N): a push or pull in a particular direction; a 10 N force left has a different effect from 10 N right.
**Acceleration** (m/s^2): rate of change of velocity; can be in the direction of motion (speeding up) or opposite (slowing down, deceleration).
**Momentum** (kg m/s): momentum = mass x velocity; it takes the direction of the velocity.
When a vector is multiplied by a scalar (e.g. mass x velocity) the answer is a vector.

callouts.p: A negative acceleration means the acceleration is opposite to the chosen positive direction.

core.p: A vector can be drawn as an **arrow**: its **length** represents the magnitude and its **direction** shows the direction of the quantity.
bullets: Choose a scale, e.g. 1 cm = 10 N.
A 40 N force would then be an arrow 4 cm long.
For forces, start the arrow at the point where the force acts on the object.
Label each arrow with the quantity and its size.
A scalar cannot be drawn as an arrow: it is just a number with a unit.

core.p: For motion along a straight line, it is easiest to choose one direction as **positive** and the opposite as **negative**.
bullets: e.g. right = +, left = -.
A ball thrown up at +8 m/s returns down at -8 m/s: same speed, different velocity.
Scalars cannot be negative in this sense: distance, speed, mass, energy and time are never given a direction.
A negative displacement means the object is on the other side of the start point.

callouts.p: For a vector in one dimension, the sign tells you the direction, not that the size is less than zero.

core.p: Because vectors have direction, you cannot just add their sizes. You must take account of direction.
bullets: Same direction: **add** the magnitudes. 6 N right + 3 N right = 9 N right.
Opposite directions: **subtract**, and the answer is in the direction of the larger one. 6 N right + 3 N left = 3 N right.
Equal and opposite: resultant is **zero**.
Scalars simply add: 6 kg + 3 kg = 9 kg every time.
Vectors at angles are added using scale drawings (covered in 9.3 to 9.5).

core.p: The spec says explain the difference **using examples**, so always pair the definition with a named quantity.
bullets: State: a vector has magnitude and direction; a scalar has magnitude only.
Give a vector example: velocity, e.g. 30 m/s north.
Give a scalar example: speed, e.g. 30 m/s.
Best answers use a matching pair to show the contrast clearly.

callouts.p: Speed is a scalar because it only has size (e.g. 12 m/s); velocity is a vector because it has size and direction (e.g. 12 m/s east).

analogy.p: Telling a friend 'my house is 2 km away' is like giving a scalar: it tells them how far but they could walk 2 km in any direction and never arrive. Saying '2 km north' is a vector: size plus direction, so they can actually find you. Where it breaks down: in the analogy the direction just helps you find a place, but in physics the direction changes the outcome itself, for example two equal forces in opposite directions cancel completely, while two equal masses always add.

The amount of matter in an object; a scalar (kg).
Mass x velocity; a vector (kg m/s).
A scalar quantity measured in joules (J).

exam.q: Which of these is a vector quantity: mass, energy, velocity, time?
model: Velocity
exam.tip: Check for direction.

exam.q: State the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity.
model: Scalar has magnitude/size only
Vector has magnitude and direction
exam.tip: Use the word 'magnitude' or 'size' in both.

exam.q: Name two scalar quantities and two vector quantities.
model: Scalars: any two from distance, speed, mass, energy, time
Vectors: any two from displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum
exam.tip: Use the spec's named examples.

exam.q: Explain why weight is a vector but mass is a scalar.
model: Weight is a force so has size and direction (downwards / towards centre of Earth)
Mass has size only / no direction
exam.tip: Give the direction of weight.

exam.q: A runner completes one lap of a 400 m circular track. State the distance travelled and the displacement.
model: Distance = 400 m
Displacement = 0 m
exam.tip: Displacement is start to finish.

exam.q: Explain why a car travelling round a roundabout at a constant speed is accelerating.
model: Direction of motion is changing
so velocity is changing (velocity is a vector)
acceleration is the rate of change of velocity
exam.tip: Link direction to velocity to acceleration.

exam.q: A cyclist travels 300 m east then 400 m west. Calculate the distance travelled and the displacement.
model: Distance = 300 + 400 = 700 m
Displacement = 400 - 300 = 100 m
west
exam.tip: Displacement needs a direction.

exam.q: Two forces act on a box: 25 N to the right and 10 N to the left. Calculate the resultant force.
model: to the right
exam.tip: Size and direction for full marks.

exam.q: Car A travels at 20 m/s north and car B at 20 m/s south. Compare their speeds and velocities.
model: Same speed (20 m/s)
Different velocities because directions are different
exam.tip: Use both words correctly.

exam.q: Explain, using examples, the difference between scalar and vector quantities. Include how vectors can be represented and combined.
model: Scalar: magnitude only
Vector: magnitude and direction
Examples: speed/distance/mass/energy (scalar) vs velocity/displacement/weight/force (vector)
Matching pair, e.g. 7 m distance vs 5 m displacement north-east
Vectors represented by arrows: length for magnitude, arrow for direction
Vectors in the same direction add; opposite directions subtract; scalars just add
Constant speed in a circle shows velocity changing while speed stays the same
exam.tip: Definitions, examples, arrows and combining, all linked.

worked.q: A dog runs 12 m east, then 5 m north. Find the distance travelled and the size of its displacement.
steps: Distance = 12 + 5 = 17 m (scalar, just add)
The displacement is the straight line from start to end, the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle
Displacement = 13 m, in a direction north of east
worked.ans: Distance 17 m; displacement 13 m north of east

worked.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 6 m/s and is caught at the same height moving at 6 m/s downwards. Taking up as positive, compare its initial and final speed and velocity, and state its displacement.
steps: Initial velocity = +6 m/s; final velocity = -6 m/s
Initial speed = final speed = 6 m/s
Velocity has changed because the direction has reversed
Start and end at the same height, so displacement = 0 m
worked.ans: Speed unchanged at 6 m/s; velocity changed from +6 m/s to -6 m/s; displacement 0 m

worked.q: Three forces act along a line on a sledge: 40 N forward from a pull, 15 N backward from friction and 5 N backward from air resistance. Find the resultant force.
steps: Take forward as positive
Total forward = +40 N
Total backward = -15 N + (-5 N) = -20 N
Resultant = 40 - 20 = +20 N

phy_edx.8.2.summary: Forces are vectors, so to work out their overall effect you must combine them taking direction into account. A free body diagram shows every force acting on one object, and adding those forces gives the single resultant force that decides whether the object accelerates. At Higher tier you also use scale vector diagrams to add forces at angles, to resolve one force into two perpendicular components, and to show equilibrium as a closed shape with zero resultant.

core.p: When several forces act on an object, they can be replaced by **one single force that has the same effect as all of them together**. This is the **resultant force** (also called the net force). Because force is a **vector**, you cannot just add the numbers: you must take account of **direction**.
bullets: The resultant force decides what happens to the motion of the object (Newton's first and second laws).
Resultant force = 0 N: the object stays at rest or keeps moving at **constant velocity**.
Resultant force not zero: the object **accelerates** in the direction of the resultant (speeds up, slows down or changes direction).
Units: newtons, N. Always give a size **and** a direction for a resultant, e.g. 30 N to the right.

callouts.p: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.

core.p: For forces that act along one straight line, pick one direction as positive and add the forces with signs. Forces in the same direction **add**; forces in opposite directions **subtract**.
bullets: Same direction: 20 N right + 15 N right = 35 N right.
Opposite directions: 50 N right and 20 N left gives 30 N right.
Equal and opposite forces (e.g. 40 N up and 40 N down) give a resultant of 0 N: the forces are **balanced**.
Do horizontal and vertical directions **separately**: vertical forces do not cancel horizontal ones.

callouts.p: Zero resultant force means no acceleration. A car on a straight motorway at a steady 30 m/s has balanced forces.

core.p: A **free body diagram** shows a single object (often drawn as a box or dot) with **every force acting on it** drawn as an arrow. Only forces acting **on** that object are included, not forces it exerts on other things.
bullets: Draw each force as an arrow starting **on the object** (usually from its centre).
Arrow **length** shows the size of the force (longer = bigger); arrow **direction** shows the direction of the force.
**Label** every arrow with the name of the force and its size if known (e.g. weight 200 N).
Typical forces: weight (down), normal contact force (perpendicular to surface), friction (opposes sliding), drag or air resistance (opposes motion), thrust, tension, upthrust.
Balanced arrows should be drawn the **same length**; an unbalanced pair should clearly differ.

callouts.p: In 'draw a free body diagram' questions marks go for correct direction, correct labels and relative lengths. Use a ruler and put arrowheads on.

fig.cap: Free body diagram of a box pushed along a floor. Weight and normal contact force are equal and opposite so the vertical resultant is zero; push (80 N) minus friction (50 N) gives a resultant of 30 N to the right, so the box accelerates to the right.

core.h: Using free body diagrams to find the resultant
core.p: Once every force is drawn, find the resultant in each direction. This tells you whether the object accelerates and which way.
bullets: Step 1: list all forces with directions.
Step 2: add vertical forces (up positive, down negative).
Step 3: add horizontal forces (e.g. right positive).
Step 4: if both totals are zero the object is in **equilibrium**; otherwise it accelerates along the resultant.
Link to F = m × a: once you know the resultant force you can find the acceleration, a = F ÷ m.

callouts.p: The resultant force, not any single force, determines the acceleration.

core.h: Examples of forces on isolated objects and systems
core.p: The spec expects you to describe the forces on everyday objects. Treat the object as isolated: draw only forces acting on it.
bullets: **Book resting on a table**: weight down, normal contact force up, equal size, resultant 0 N.
**Skydiver at terminal velocity**: weight down, air resistance up, equal, so constant speed.
**Car accelerating**: driving force forward bigger than drag + friction backward; weight balanced by normal force.
**Hanging lamp**: weight down, tension in cable up, equal, so stationary.
**Boat floating**: weight down balanced by upthrust from the water.
**Object on a slope**: weight vertically down, normal contact force perpendicular to the slope, friction up along the slope.

core.h: Vector diagrams: adding forces at an angle (HT)
core.p: When forces are **not along the same line**, you find the resultant using a **vector diagram** drawn to scale. Arrows are joined **tip to tail**, and the resultant goes from the **start of the first arrow to the tip of the last**.
bullets: Choose a sensible **scale**, e.g. 1 cm = 10 N, and write it down.
Draw the first force arrow to scale in the correct direction (use a protractor).
Draw the second arrow starting from the **tip** of the first.
Draw the resultant from the **tail of the first** to the **tip of the last**.
Measure its length and convert using the scale to get the size; measure the angle for the direction.
Order does not matter: adding A then B gives the same resultant as B then A (parallelogram).

callouts.p: Joining tip to tip, or measuring the resultant in cm and forgetting to convert back to newtons.

core.p: When two forces are at **right angles**, the vector diagram is a right-angled triangle, so you can check the scale drawing with Pythagoras and trigonometry.
bullets: Size: resultant² = F1² + F2².
Direction: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent, so θ = tan⁻¹(40 ÷ 30) = 53°.
Edexcel usually asks for a **scale drawing**; calculation is a useful check and accuracy of about ±1 N or ±2° is normally allowed.
The resultant of two forces is always between (F1 - F2) and (F1 + F2).

core.p: **Resolving** is the reverse of adding: one force is **split into two perpendicular components** (usually horizontal and vertical) which together have the same effect as the original force.
bullets: Draw the force to scale as the **hypotenuse** of a right-angled triangle.
Draw horizontal and vertical lines from its ends to make the other two sides.
Measure each side and convert using the scale to get each component.
Check by calculation: horizontal = F cos θ, vertical = F sin θ (θ measured from the horizontal).
Why resolve? It lets you see how much of a force acts in a useful direction, e.g. how much of a pull on a sledge rope moves it forwards and how much lifts it.

callouts.p: Splitting a single force into two components at right angles to each other that together have the same effect as the original force.

core.p: On a slope, it is helpful to resolve the weight into a component **along the slope** and a component **perpendicular to the slope**.
bullets: Component along the slope pulls the object down the slope; friction acts up the slope to oppose it.
Component perpendicular to the slope is balanced by the **normal contact force**.
Steeper slope: larger component along the slope, smaller perpendicular component.
If the object rests still, friction exactly equals the component of weight along the slope.

core.p: An object is in **equilibrium** when the resultant force on it is **zero**. On a vector diagram, forces in equilibrium joined tip to tail form a **closed shape** (a closed triangle for three forces), because you end up back where you started.
bullets: Two forces in equilibrium: equal size, opposite direction, same line.
Three forces in equilibrium: arrows drawn tip to tail make a **closed triangle**.
If the shape does not close, the gap is the resultant force; the force needed for equilibrium is equal and opposite to that gap.
Alternative check: resolve all forces horizontally and vertically; each set must add to zero.
Example: a picture hanging from two angled strings; the two tensions and the weight form a closed triangle.

callouts.p: Equilibrium means resultant force = 0, so the object is stationary or moving at constant velocity.

core.p: Most marks in vector diagram questions come from careful drawing. Accuracy matters.
bullets: Use a sharp pencil, a ruler and a protractor.
Choose a scale that makes the diagram **as large as possible** on the grid; larger diagrams reduce percentage error.
Mark arrowheads on every vector and label each with its force.
State the scale, the measured length and the converted force in your answer.
Give the direction as an angle from a stated reference (e.g. 37° above the horizontal).

core.p: The resultant force is the bridge between forces and motion in Topic 2 (Newton's laws).
bullets: Resultant forward: object speeds up.
Resultant backward (opposite to motion): object slows down.
Resultant at right angles to motion: object changes direction (e.g. circular motion).
Resultant zero: constant velocity or at rest.
a = F ÷ m: the bigger the resultant force or smaller the mass, the bigger the acceleration.

analogy.p: Adding vectors tip to tail is like following directions on a treasure map: walk 30 paces east, then 40 paces north. However twisty the route, the straight line from where you started to where you end up (50 paces) is the resultant. Resolving is the reverse: describing one diagonal walk as 'so far east plus so far north'. Equilibrium is a walk that brings you back to your starting point. It breaks down because forces all act at once on the object, not one after another, and a force is not a distance: the order of drawing is just a bookkeeping trick.

terms.d: A quantity with both magnitude (size) and direction, e.g. force, velocity, displacement.
A quantity with magnitude only, e.g. mass, speed, energy.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
Another name for resultant force.
A diagram of one object showing all the forces acting on it as labelled arrows.
Forces whose resultant is zero, so there is no change in motion.
Forces with a non-zero resultant, causing acceleration.
The state of an object when the resultant force on it is zero.
A scale drawing in which force arrows are joined tip to tail to find a resultant.
Method of adding vectors: each new arrow starts at the head of the previous one.
Splitting one force into two perpendicular components with the same combined effect.
One of the perpendicular parts (e.g. horizontal or vertical) of a resolved force.
The ratio linking arrow length to force size in a scale drawing, e.g. 1 cm = 10 N.
The force from a surface on an object, acting at right angles to the surface.
The gravitational force on an object, acting vertically downwards: W = m × g.
A contact force that opposes relative sliding of two surfaces.

phy_edx.8.3.summary: A moment is the turning effect of a force about a pivot, calculated as force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, in newton metres (N m). Bigger forces and bigger distances give bigger moments, which is why long levers and spanners make turning easier. When an object is balanced, the principle of moments applies: the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments, which lets you calculate unknown forces and distances, including support forces on beams.

core.p: A force can make an object **turn about a pivot** (a fixed point). The **turning effect** of a force is called its **moment**. Opening a door, using a spanner, a see-saw and a wheelbarrow all involve moments.
bullets: Forces cause rotation when they act on an object that is fixed at a pivot (or can turn about some point) and the line of action of the force does **not** pass through the pivot.
A moment can be **clockwise** or **anticlockwise**.
If the line of action of a force passes through the pivot, its moment is **zero**: it cannot turn the object.
Examples: door handle far from hinges, spanner turning a nut, crowbar, wheelbarrow, scissors, crane, see-saw.

callouts.p: The turning effect of a force about a pivot.

core.p: The size of a moment depends on the size of the force and how far from the pivot it acts, measured at right angles to the force.
bullets: **moment of a force (N m) = force (N) × distance normal to the direction of the force (m)**
Symbols: M = F × d.
Unit: **newton metre, N m** (not N/m, and not the joule even though the base units match).
Distance must be the **perpendicular** (normal) distance from the pivot to the **line of action** of the force.
Convert cm to m first if the answer must be in N m (e.g. 30 cm = 0.30 m).

callouts.p: moment of a force = force × distance normal to the direction of the force. You must recall this; it is not on the equation sheet.

core.p: Doubling the distance from the pivot doubles the moment for the same force. This is why long handles make turning easier.
bullets: A long spanner gives a bigger moment for the same force, so a stiff nut is easier to undo.
Door handles are placed **far from the hinges** so a small force gives a large enough moment.
Pushing a door near the hinge needs a much larger force for the same moment.
To get the **maximum** moment, push at right angles to the lever and as far from the pivot as possible.

core.h: Forces at an angle: perpendicular distance
core.p: If the force is not at 90° to the lever, the distance you use is the **perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action** of the force, which is shorter than the length of the lever.
bullets: Extend the force arrow into a line (its line of action).
Draw a line from the pivot that meets the line of action at 90°: that length is d.
Angled forces therefore give a **smaller moment** than the same force at right angles.
Edexcel questions usually give the perpendicular distance or have forces at 90°; read the diagram carefully.

callouts.p: Using the length of the bar when the force is at an angle. Only the perpendicular distance counts.

core.p: When several forces act, some try to turn the object clockwise and some anticlockwise. Work out each moment about the **same pivot**.
bullets: Look at each force and imagine which way it would turn the object on its own.
Add all the clockwise moments together; add all the anticlockwise moments together.
If they are unequal, the object turns in the direction of the larger total.
The resultant moment = larger total - smaller total.

core.p: For an object that is **balanced** (not turning, in rotational equilibrium), the turning effects cancel out.
bullets: **sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments** about any pivot, for an object in equilibrium.
This lets you find an unknown force or distance.
Example: see-saw with 400 N at 1.5 m left and 600 N at 1.0 m right: 400 × 1.5 = 600 N m and 600 × 1.0 = 600 N m, so it balances.
A heavier person must sit **closer** to the pivot to balance a lighter person.

callouts.p: For an object in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that pivot.

fig.cap: A balanced see-saw. The anticlockwise moment (400 N × 1.5 m = 600 N m) equals the clockwise moment (600 N × 1.0 m = 600 N m), so the principle of moments is satisfied and it does not turn.

core.p: For an object to be completely balanced, two things must be true.
bullets: The **resultant force** is zero (forces up = forces down, forces left = forces right), so it does not accelerate.
The **resultant moment** is zero (clockwise = anticlockwise), so it does not start to rotate.
Both conditions are needed: two equal and opposite forces not in line form a **couple** that turns the object even though the resultant force is zero.

core.p: The weight of an object acts as if it is concentrated at a single point, the **centre of gravity** (centre of mass). For a uniform beam this is at the **middle**.
bullets: A uniform beam's weight acts at its midpoint, so it produces a moment if the pivot is not at the middle.
An object hanging freely comes to rest with its centre of gravity directly below the pivot (then the weight has no moment).
Remember to include the weight of the beam itself in moment calculations if it is given.

core.p: When a beam rests on two supports, both supports push up. Use the principle of moments, taking moments **about one support** so that support's force has zero moment and drops out.
bullets: Step 1: choose a pivot at one support (the unknown force there has no moment).
Step 2: write clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments and solve for the other support force.
Step 3: use forces up = forces down to get the first support force.
The support **nearer to a heavy load** pushes up with the larger force.
Check: the two support forces must add up to the total weight.

core.p: Many questions ask for a force or distance rather than the moment.
bullets: F = M ÷ d
d = M ÷ F
For balancing problems: F1 × d1 = F2 × d2, so d2 = (F1 × d1) ÷ F2.
Always show the equation, the substitution and the answer with unit.

core.p: A metre rule balanced on a pivot with masses hung from it lets you test the principle.
bullets: Balance the metre rule at its centre (50 cm mark) so its own weight has no moment.
Hang a known mass on one side at a measured distance; move another mass on the other side until the rule balances.
Weight = mass × g (g = 10 N/kg); calculate clockwise and anticlockwise moments.
They should be equal within experimental error.
Sources of error: reading distances to the centre of each mass hanger, friction at the pivot.

core.p: Engineers use moments to make tasks easier and to keep structures stable.
bullets: Cranes use a **counterweight** to balance the moment of the load and stop the crane toppling.
A wheelbarrow lets a small upward force at long handles lift a heavy load near the wheel (pivot).
Bridges and shelves: support forces are calculated with the principle of moments.
Objects **topple** when the line of action of the weight falls outside the base, giving an unbalanced moment.

analogy.t: A tug of war on a merry-go-round
analogy.p: Imagine children pushing a merry-go-round in opposite directions. A push far from the centre counts for more than the same push near the centre, so a small child at the edge can beat a big child near the middle. The merry-go-round stays still only when the total turning push each way is equal, just like clockwise and anticlockwise moments balancing. It breaks down because children push along the edge (tangent) while many moment questions involve forces at other angles, where only the perpendicular distance to the line of action counts, and a real merry-go-round also has friction at its axle.

terms.d: The turning effect of a force about a pivot.
The fixed point about which an object turns (also called the fulcrum).
The unit of moment: a force of 1 N acting 1 m from the pivot.
The shortest distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, at 90° to the force.
The straight line along which a force acts, extended in both directions.
A moment tending to turn an object in the direction clock hands move.
A moment tending to turn an object opposite to clock hands.
For an object in equilibrium, total clockwise moment about a pivot equals total anticlockwise moment about that pivot.
Resultant force and resultant moment are both zero, so the object neither accelerates nor starts to turn.
The difference between total clockwise and total anticlockwise moments.
The point through which the whole weight of an object can be considered to act.
A beam whose mass is evenly spread, so its centre of gravity is at its midpoint.
The upward force a support exerts on a beam resting on it.
A weight used to provide a balancing moment, e.g. on a crane.
Two equal, opposite, parallel forces not in line that produce turning without a resultant force.

mistakes.w: Uses the length of the lever when the force is at an angle.
mistakes.r: Use the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.

mistakes.w: Uses distance in cm and gives answer in N m.
mistakes.r: Convert cm to m first (or give N cm clearly).

mistakes.r: Moment = force × perpendicular distance.

exam.q: State the equation linking moment, force and distance.
model: moment = force × distance normal to the direction of the force
exam.tip: Say 'normal' or 'perpendicular' distance.

exam.q: Give the unit of a moment.
model: N m (newton metre)
exam.tip: Not N/m.

exam.q: A force of 25 N is applied at right angles to a spanner 0.30 m from the nut. Calculate the moment.
exam.tip: Show substitution then answer with unit.

exam.q: Explain why door handles are placed as far as possible from the hinges.
model: Larger distance from pivot gives larger moment
So a smaller force is needed to open the door
exam.tip: Link distance, moment and force.

exam.q: State the principle of moments.
model: For an object in equilibrium / balanced
sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments (about a pivot)
exam.tip: Use the word 'sum' and the equilibrium condition.

exam.q: A child of weight 300 N sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a see-saw. Calculate how far from the pivot her father, weight 800 N, must sit to balance it.
exam.tip: Equate the two moments, then rearrange.

exam.q: A uniform plank 4.0 m long weighing 200 N rests on supports at each end. A 600 N person stands 1.0 m from the left end. Calculate the force from the right support.
model: Take moments about left support
Clockwise moments = 600 × 1.0 + 200 × 2.0 = 1000 N m
exam.tip: Choose a pivot at a support to remove one unknown.

exam.q: Explain why the force on the right support in the previous question is less than the force on the left support.
model: The person is nearer the left support
So the left support must provide more of the upward force / total of 800 N shared unequally (left 550 N)
exam.tip: Use a number check: the two forces add to the total weight.

exam.q: A metre rule is balanced at its centre. Describe how you could use it to investigate the principle of moments.
model: Balance rule on pivot at the 50 cm mark
Hang a known mass/weight at a measured distance on one side
Hang a second mass on the other side and adjust its position until the rule balances
Measure distances from the pivot to the centre of each mass
Calculate weights using W = m × g and moments using F × d
Repeat with different masses/positions and compare clockwise and anticlockwise moments, which should be equal
exam.tip: Give a clear method in order with measurements and the calculation.

exam.q: A crane has a counterweight. Explain why the crane does not topple when lifting a load.
model: The load produces a moment about the tower/pivot
The counterweight produces an opposite moment
When the moments are equal the resultant moment is zero so it does not rotate/topple
exam.tip: Name both moments and their directions.

worked.q: A 450 N force is needed to lift a wheelbarrow handle 1.2 m from the wheel axle. Calculate the moment of this force.
steps: Moment = force × perpendicular distance

worked.q: On a balanced metre rule pivoted at its centre, a 2.0 N weight hangs 30 cm left of the pivot. Where must a 1.5 N weight hang on the right?
steps: Anticlockwise moment = 2.0 × 0.30 = 0.60 N m
Clockwise moment = 1.5 × d
Principle of moments: 1.5 × d = 0.60
worked.ans: 0.40 m (40 cm) right of the pivot.

worked.q: A uniform 2.0 m beam of weight 200 N rests on supports A (left end) and B (right end). A 300 N load is 0.5 m from A. Find both support forces.
steps: Take moments about A so R(A) has no moment.
Anticlockwise moment = R(B) × 2.0
Forces up = forces down: R(A) + 175 = 500, so R(A) = 325 N

phy_edx.8.4.summary: Levers and gears transmit the rotational effect of a force (its moment) and can act as force multipliers. A lever lets a small effort applied far from the pivot balance a large load close to the pivot, because the moments are equal. Meshing gears push on each other with equal forces at the teeth, so a larger gear gets a larger moment but turns more slowly, a smaller gear gets a smaller moment but turns faster, and each meshing pair turns in opposite directions.

core.h: Levers and gears transmit turning effects
core.p: Levers and gears are simple machines that **transmit the rotational effect of a force** (its moment) from one place to another. They let a **small force** produce a **large turning effect**, or let a slow rotation produce a fast one. Both work using **moments**.
bullets: A lever transmits a moment through a rigid bar turning about a pivot.
Gears transmit a moment from one rotating shaft to another through interlocking teeth.
Neither creates energy: if force is multiplied, distance moved is reduced (ignoring friction, work in = work out).
Machines that multiply force are called **force multipliers**.

callouts.p: Explain how levers and gears transmit the rotational effects of forces.

core.p: Every lever has three key points.
bullets: **Pivot** (fulcrum): the point the lever turns about.
**Effort**: the force you apply.
**Load**: the force the lever exerts on the object being moved (equal to the object's weight or resistance).
**Effort distance**: perpendicular distance from pivot to line of action of the effort.
**Load distance**: perpendicular distance from pivot to line of action of the load.

core.p: Using the principle of moments, when a lever is balanced: **effort × effort distance = load × load distance**. If the effort is applied much further from the pivot than the load, a **small effort balances a large load**.
bullets: Example: crowbar with effort 1.2 m from pivot and load 0.2 m from pivot.
Effort × 1.2 = 600 × 0.2 = 120 N m, so effort = 100 N.
The effort is 6 times smaller than the load because its distance is 6 times bigger.
Trade-off: the effort end moves 6 times further than the load end.
The longer the handle, the smaller the effort needed.

callouts.p: Always explain using moments: 'the effort is further from the pivot, so a smaller force gives the same moment as the load'.

fig.cap: A crowbar used as a lever. The 100 N effort acts 1.2 m from the pivot and the 600 N load 0.2 m from it: both moments are 120 N m, so the small effort balances the large load.

core.p: Many tools are levers. Spotting the pivot, effort and load is a common exam task.
bullets: **Crowbar**: pivot near the load; long handle for the effort.
**Wheelbarrow**: pivot at the wheel axle, load in the tray, effort at the handles further from the axle.
**Spanner**: pivot at the nut, effort at the end of the handle.
**Scissors and pliers**: pivot at the joint; cutting near the pivot gives a larger force.
**Bottle opener**: pivot at the top of the cap, effort at the handle.
**Forearm**: pivot at the elbow; muscle effort close to pivot, so larger force but faster hand movement (a distance multiplier).

core.p: A **gear** is a wheel with **teeth** around its edge. When two gears **mesh** (teeth interlock), turning one makes the other turn.
bullets: The gear you turn (attached to the motor, pedal or handle) is the **driver** or input gear.
The gear it turns is the **driven** or output gear.
Meshing gears turn in **opposite directions**.
The teeth push on each other with **equal and opposite forces** at the point of contact.

core.h: Why a bigger driven gear gives a bigger moment
core.p: At the teeth, the force on each gear is the same size. But moment = force × distance from the axle (radius). The larger gear has a larger radius, so the **same force gives a bigger moment** on the larger gear.
bullets: Small driver turning a large driven gear: **moment increases**, driven gear turns **more slowly**.
Large driver turning a small driven gear: **moment decreases**, driven gear turns **faster**.
If the driven gear has twice the number of teeth, it has about twice the radius, so the moment roughly doubles and it turns at half the speed.
This is the same trade-off as a lever: more turning effect means less rotation.

callouts.p: Small gear driving a large gear: bigger moment, lower speed. Large gear driving a small gear: smaller moment, higher speed.

fig.cap: A 10-tooth driver turning a 20-tooth driven gear. The gears turn in opposite directions; the larger driven gear turns at half the speed but its moment is doubled because the same tooth force acts at twice the radius.

core.p: Comparing the number of teeth tells you how speed and moment change.
bullets: Gear ratio = teeth on driven gear ÷ teeth on driver gear.
Turns of driven gear = turns of driver ÷ gear ratio.
Moment on driven gear ≈ moment on driver × gear ratio (ignoring friction).
Example: 10-tooth driver, 30-tooth driven: ratio 3. Driver turns 3 times for every 1 turn of driven gear; moment is about 3 times larger.
Teeth count is proportional to circumference, and therefore to radius, because teeth on meshing gears are the same size.

core.p: Two meshing gears turn in opposite directions. To make the output turn the **same way** as the input, a third gear (an **idler**) is placed between them.
bullets: Gear 1 clockwise, gear 2 anticlockwise, gear 3 clockwise.
An idler gear does not change the overall speed or moment between the first and last gears; it just changes direction (or bridges a gap).
In a chain of gears, count how many there are: odd number gives the same direction as the driver, even number gives the opposite.

fig.cap: A train of three equal gears. The middle idler gear reverses the direction so the driven gear turns clockwise like the driver, at the same speed.

core.p: Gears can also be used to increase speed at the cost of turning effect.
bullets: A **large driver** turning a **small driven gear** makes the output spin faster.
Bicycles: a large front chainring and small rear sprocket give high speed (top gear) but need a bigger force on the pedals.
For hill climbing, a small front gear and large rear gear give a larger moment at the wheel, so it is easier to pedal, but slower.
Gears in a car gearbox: low gear for big moment when starting, high gear for speed.

fig.cap: A large 20-tooth driver turning a small 10-tooth driven gear. The output turns twice as fast but its moment is halved, as in a bicycle's top gear.

core.p: Gears appear in many machines where turning effects must be changed.
bullets: Car gearboxes and bicycle gears.
Electric drills and food mixers (motor turns fast; gears give a bigger moment at lower speed).
Clocks and watches (to make hands turn at different rates).
Winches and hand whisks.
Wind turbines (gears increase the slow rotation of the blades to a fast rotation for the generator).

core.p: Levers and gears do not give you free energy. The work done by the effort is at least the work done on the load.
bullets: Work done = force × distance moved along the line of the force.
A force multiplier reduces the force needed but the effort moves further.
Friction at pivots and between gear teeth wastes energy as heating, so real machines are less than 100% efficient.
Lubricating gears reduces friction and unwanted energy transfer.

callouts.p: Saying a lever or gear 'creates more energy' or 'reduces the work done'. It reduces the force needed, not the energy.

core.h: Writing explanations for levers and gears
core.p: Exam answers on this point are usually explanations. Use a moment-based chain of reasoning.
bullets: State the equation: moment = force × distance (from pivot/axle).
Identify which distance is bigger (effort distance or radius of driven gear).
Conclude that the same moment needs a smaller force, or the same force gives a bigger moment.
Mention the trade-off in distance moved or speed.
For gears, mention opposite directions of rotation where relevant.

analogy.t: Opening a heavy door with a long handle
analogy.p: A lever is like pushing a heavy gate: push near the hinge and it barely moves, push at the far edge and it swings easily, because the same moment needs less force further out. Gears are like two people of different sizes walking side by side holding hands around a roundabout: the person on the outside (big gear) covers more distance per turn, so turns fewer times but with more leverage. It breaks down because people can change speed independently, whereas meshing teeth force the edges to move at exactly the same speed, and the analogy hides the reversal of direction between meshing gears.

terms.d: A rigid bar that turns about a pivot, used to transmit a moment and often to multiply force.
The fixed point about which a lever or gear turns.
The force applied to a lever or machine by the user.
The force that the lever or machine has to overcome or move.
A machine where the output force is larger than the input force.
The turning effect of a force: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot.
A toothed wheel that transmits rotation and moments to another gear.
When the teeth of two gears interlock so that one turns the other.
The input gear, turned by a motor, pedal or handle.
The output gear, turned by the driver.
A gear placed between two others to make them turn in the same direction.
Number of teeth on driven gear divided by number of teeth on driver gear.
A series of meshing gears.
The tendency of a force to turn an object, measured by its moment.

mistakes.w: Meshing gears turn in the same direction.
mistakes.r: Two meshing gears turn in opposite directions.

mistakes.w: A larger driven gear turns faster.
mistakes.r: A larger driven gear turns more slowly but with a larger moment.

mistakes.w: A lever creates extra energy / reduces the work.
mistakes.r: It reduces the force needed; the effort moves a larger distance.

mistakes.w: A lever works because the effort is close to the pivot.
mistakes.r: The effort is far from the pivot so a small force gives a large moment.

mistakes.w: Gears change the force at the teeth.
mistakes.r: Forces at the teeth are equal; the different radii change the moment.

mistakes.w: Explains without mentioning moments.
mistakes.r: Use moment = force × distance in the explanation.

mistakes.w: An idler gear changes the speed of the output.
mistakes.r: An idler changes direction only; speed depends on the first and last gears.

mistakes.w: Confuses load and effort on a wheelbarrow.
mistakes.r: Load is in the tray, effort at the handles, pivot at the wheel.

exam.q: State what is meant by a force multiplier.
model: A device where the output force is larger than the input force (effort).
exam.tip: Levers and gears can both be force multipliers.

exam.q: Two gears mesh. The driver turns clockwise. State the direction of the driven gear.
model: Anticlockwise
exam.tip: Meshing gears turn opposite ways.

exam.q: Explain why a long-handled lever makes it easier to lift a heavy load.
model: Effort is a larger distance from the pivot
So a smaller force gives the moment needed to balance the load
exam.tip: Mention distance and moment.

exam.q: A crowbar has the load 0.15 m from the pivot and the effort 0.90 m from the pivot. The load is 540 N. Calculate the effort needed.
model: = 81 N m
Effort = 90 N
exam.tip: Use the principle of moments.

exam.q: A small gear drives a large gear. Explain how the moment and speed of the large gear compare with the small gear.
model: Force at the teeth is the same on both gears
Large gear has a larger radius
So the moment (force × radius) on the large gear is larger
The large gear turns more slowly
exam.tip: Four separate points for four marks.

exam.q: A driver gear has 12 teeth and the driven gear has 36 teeth. The driver makes 60 turns. Calculate the number of turns of the driven gear.
model: Ratio 36 ÷ 12 = 3
60 ÷ 3 = 20 turns
exam.tip: Bigger driven gear turns fewer times.

exam.q: Explain why a third gear may be placed between two gears.
model: Two meshing gears turn in opposite directions
A middle (idler) gear makes the first and last gears turn in the same direction
exam.tip: Name it an idler gear.

exam.q: Identify the pivot, effort and load for a wheelbarrow.

Load: weight of contents in the tray
Effort: upward force at the handles

model: Pedal cranks act as levers: the force on the pedal at a distance from the axle produces a moment
Front chainring and rear sprocket act as gears linked by the chain
Choosing a small front gear and large rear gear

worked.q: A wheelbarrow carries a 900 N load 0.40 m from the wheel axle. The handles are 1.50 m from the axle. Calculate the upward force needed at the handles.

Effort = 360 ÷ 1.50

steps: Gear ratio = 45 ÷ 15 = 3
Force at teeth is equal; radius of driven gear is 3 times larger
Moment on driven gear = 2.0 × 3 = 6.0 N m
Speed of driven gear = 1/3 of driver; turns in opposite direction

worked.q: Explain how a pair of scissors acts as a lever to cut thick card.
steps: The pivot is the rivet joining the blades.
The effort is applied at the handles, a large distance from the pivot.
Moment = force × distance, so a small effort gives a large moment.
Placing the card close to the pivot means a small load distance, so the cutting force on the card is large.
worked.ans: Large effort distance and small load distance make the scissors a force multiplier.

phy_edx.8.5.summary: Whenever surfaces rub together, **friction** does work and transfers energy from the kinetic store of the moving parts to the **thermal store** of the parts and the surroundings. This energy is usually **wasted** (dissipated) and it lowers the **efficiency** of a machine. A **lubricant** such as oil or grease forms a thin layer between the surfaces, which **reduces friction** so less energy is wasted by heating, the machine runs cooler, wears out more slowly and more of the input energy is transferred usefully.

core.p: Edexcel 9.10 asks you to **explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfer**, with lubrication as the named method. To score full marks you must link: friction between surfaces, work done against friction, energy transferred to the **thermal store**, energy being **dissipated** to the surroundings, and how a lubricant reduces that friction.
bullets: Name the force: **friction** between surfaces in contact that move past each other.
Name the store: energy is transferred to the **thermal energy store** of the surfaces and surroundings.
Name the effect: the surfaces **heat up**; the energy is **wasted** (not useful).
Name the fix: a **lubricant** (oil, grease) reduces friction, so **less energy is wasted**.
Name the consequence: **efficiency increases**, parts last longer, less overheating.

callouts.p: Surfaces rub -> friction -> work done against friction -> surfaces heat up -> energy dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings -> lubricant reduces friction -> less energy wasted -> higher efficiency.

core.p: Even surfaces that look smooth are covered in tiny bumps and hollows when magnified. When one surface slides over another, these bumps catch on each other and resist the motion. This resistive force is **friction**, and it always acts **opposite to the direction of motion** (or attempted motion).
bullets: Friction is a **contact force**: it only acts when the surfaces touch.
It acts **parallel** to the surfaces and **opposes relative motion**.
Rougher surfaces and surfaces pressed together harder generally give more friction.
The bumps catching and deforming make the particles in the surfaces vibrate more, which is why they get hotter.

callouts.p: A force that opposes the relative motion of two surfaces in contact.

core.h: Work done against friction heats things up
core.p: To keep a part moving against friction, a force has to be applied through a distance, so **work is done against friction**. Work done is energy transferred (work done = force x distance moved in the direction of the force). Here the energy goes from the **kinetic store** of the moving part into the **thermal store** of the surfaces, which warm up.
bullets: Work done (J) = force (N) x distance (m), so a bigger friction force or longer distance means more energy wasted.
Rub your hands together: they get warm. That is work done against friction.
Brakes on a car deliberately use friction to transfer kinetic energy to the thermal store of the brake discs and pads.
In bearings, gears, axles and engines this heating is **unwanted**.

callouts.p: Higher-scoring answers say 'work is done against friction' rather than just 'friction makes heat'.

core.p: Energy transferred to the thermal store by friction spreads out into the surroundings. We say it is **dissipated**: it becomes so spread out that it can no longer be used to do anything useful. Energy is never destroyed (conservation of energy), but it ends up in a less useful form.
bullets: **Conservation of energy**: total energy in = useful energy out + wasted energy out.
Dissipated energy warms the surroundings very slightly and cannot easily be recovered.
Noise (sound) from grinding parts is another wasted transfer that also ends up heating the surroundings.
Unwanted energy transfer = wasted energy = energy not transferred to a useful store.

callouts.p: Energy that has spread out into the surroundings, usually by heating, so it is no longer useful.

core.p: A **lubricant** is a substance, usually a liquid such as oil or a thick semi-solid such as grease, that is put between two surfaces that move against each other. It forms a thin layer that **keeps the surfaces apart**, so the bumps no longer catch on each other and the surfaces slide over the liquid instead.
bullets: Common lubricants: **oil** (engines, bike chains), **grease** (hinges, wheel bearings, axles), graphite powder (locks).
The layer fills the gaps and **separates** the surfaces.
Liquid layers slide over each other easily, so the resistive force is much smaller.
Lubricants can also carry heat away from the hot parts (e.g. engine oil circulates).

callouts.p: Putting a substance such as oil or grease between moving surfaces to reduce friction between them.

core.h: How lubrication reduces unwanted energy transfer
core.p: Because the lubricant reduces the friction force, **less work is done against friction** for the same movement. So less energy is transferred to the thermal store of the parts, and **less energy is wasted**. More of the input energy goes to the useful store (for example, the kinetic store of a wheel).
bullets: Lower friction force -> less work done against friction (W = F x d).
Less energy transferred to thermal store -> parts stay **cooler**.
More energy transferred usefully -> **higher efficiency**.
For the same useful output, less input energy (fuel or electricity) is needed, saving money and reducing emissions.

callouts.p: Lubrication reduces friction between moving surfaces, so less energy is wasted by heating and the efficiency of the machine increases.

core.p: Efficiency tells you what fraction of the energy supplied is transferred usefully. Lubrication does not change the input energy; it changes how much of it is wasted. Less waste means a larger useful output, so efficiency goes up.
bullets: efficiency = (useful energy transferred by the device) / (total energy supplied to the device)
Efficiency can be given as a decimal (0 to 1) or a percentage (multiply by 100).
Efficiency can never be greater than 1 (100%) because energy cannot be created.
No real machine with moving parts is 100% efficient: friction can be reduced but never completely removed.

callouts.p: A lubricant does not add energy or make the input larger. It only reduces the energy wasted, so a larger share of the input is useful.

core.p: Lubrication appears wherever parts rotate or slide. In the exam you may be asked to apply the idea to a context you have not seen before, so learn the pattern rather than a list.
bullets: **Car engine**: oil between pistons and cylinder walls reduces friction, stops overheating and seizing.
**Bicycle chain and gears**: oil reduces friction between chain links and sprocket teeth, so the cyclist wastes less energy.
**Door hinges**: grease stops squeaking (sound is wasted energy) and makes the door easier to open.
**Wheel bearings and axles**: grease reduces friction so wheels spin freely.
**Machines in factories**: regular oiling keeps efficiency high and reduces wear.

core.p: Reducing friction does more than save energy. Exam questions often ask for a second benefit, so be ready to give one.
bullets: **Less wear**: the surfaces do not grind away, so parts last longer.
**Less overheating**: parts that get too hot can expand, distort or seize (jam).
**Quieter**: less vibration and noise, which is also wasted energy.
**Cheaper to run**: less fuel or electricity needed for the same useful work.

callouts.p: If asked for two benefits, give two different ideas, such as 'less energy wasted so higher efficiency' and 'less wear so the parts last longer'.

core.p: Not all friction is bad. Friction between tyres and the road lets a car accelerate, steer and brake, and friction in brakes transfers kinetic energy to the thermal store to slow a vehicle down. You would **never** lubricate these surfaces.
bullets: Brake pads and discs: friction is the useful effect.
Tyres on the road: grip comes from friction.
Shoes on the floor: friction stops you slipping.
Oil spilled on a road is dangerous because it reduces useful friction.

callouts.p: Read the question: lubrication reduces unwanted energy transfer in moving machine parts, but would be dangerous on brakes or tyres.

core.h: Other ways to reduce unwanted energy transfer
core.p: Lubrication is the method named in this spec point, but questions may ask you to compare it with other ways of reducing wasted energy, which you meet elsewhere in the course.
bullets: **Thermal insulation** (e.g. loft insulation, cavity walls) reduces unwanted energy transfer by heating through walls.
**Streamlining** reduces air resistance (drag), which is another friction-like force.
Using **wheels and bearings** (rolling instead of sliding) reduces friction.
Tightening loose parts reduces vibration and sound.

core.p: Six-mark explain questions on wasted energy reward a logical sequence of linked points. Use the key words and always say where the energy goes.
bullets: Start with the cause: friction between moving surfaces.
Say what happens: work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal store.
Say it is wasted / dissipated to the surroundings.
Explain the lubricant: forms a layer between surfaces, reduces friction.
Finish with the effect: less energy wasted, efficiency increases, parts last longer.

callouts.p: Say 'energy transferred to the thermal store' or 'energy transferred by heating', not 'heat energy is produced'.

analogy.t: Ice skates on a film of water
analogy.p: Dragging a box across a gravel path is hard work: the stones catch on the box, and your effort turns into warmth and noise. Slide the same box over a sheet of wet ice and it glides, because a thin liquid layer separates the surfaces. Oil in an engine is that wet layer: it stops the bumps catching, so your effort goes into motion rather than heating. Where it breaks down: an ice film forms because of pressure and melting, while engine oil is added deliberately and must be topped up; also, lubrication never removes friction completely, and the oil itself has some resistance (it still warms up).

Energy transferred to the store that the device is designed to fill.

A force that opposes motion, such as friction or air resistance.

mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction; it cannot remove it entirely, so some energy is still wasted.

mistakes.w: Friction destroys energy.
mistakes.r: Energy is not destroyed; work done against friction transfers it to the thermal store of the surroundings, where it is dissipated.

mistakes.w: Lubrication gives the machine more energy.
mistakes.r: It reduces the energy wasted, so a greater proportion of the input energy is transferred usefully.

mistakes.r: Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal store / energy is transferred by heating.

mistakes.w: Lubrication increases efficiency (with no reason).

exam.q: State the name of the force that causes moving parts in a machine to heat up.
model: Friction.
exam.tip: One word answer; do not write 'heat'.

exam.q: Name one substance used as a lubricant.
model: Oil / grease / graphite.
exam.tip: Any one correct example.

exam.q: State which energy store increases when two surfaces rub together.
model: Thermal (energy store) of the surfaces / surroundings.
exam.tip: Say thermal store, not 'heat'.

exam.q: Explain why a bicycle chain gets warm when the bicycle is ridden for a long time.
model: Friction between the chain and the gears / between moving parts.
Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal store (of the chain).
exam.tip: Two marks: name the cause and say where the energy goes.

exam.q: Explain how oiling the chain makes the bicycle more efficient.
model: Oil reduces friction (between chain and gears).
So less energy is wasted / transferred to the thermal store.
So a greater proportion of the input energy is transferred usefully (to the kinetic store).
exam.tip: Link each step with 'so'.

exam.q: Give two benefits of lubricating the moving parts of a machine.
model: Less energy wasted / higher efficiency.
Less wear / parts last longer / less overheating / quieter.
exam.tip: Two different ideas are needed.

exam.q: A motor is supplied with 500 J of energy and transfers 350 J usefully. Calculate its efficiency.
model: efficiency = 350 / 500
exam.tip: Efficiency has no unit.

exam.q: After the motor's bearings are greased, it transfers 420 J usefully from the same 500 J input. Calculate the energy wasted before and after greasing, and explain the change.
model: Before: 500 - 350 = 150 J wasted.
After: 500 - 420 = 80 J wasted.
Grease reduces friction in the bearings.
So less work is done against friction / less energy transferred to the thermal store.
exam.tip: Use conservation of energy for the wasted energy.

exam.q: Explain why lubricant should not be applied to a bicycle's brake blocks.
model: Brakes rely on friction to slow the bicycle / transfer kinetic energy to the thermal store.
Lubricant would reduce this friction, so the brakes would not work well / it would be dangerous.
exam.tip: Friction is the useful effect in brakes.

exam.q: Car engines contain many moving parts. Explain how energy is wasted in an engine and how lubrication reduces this waste. Refer to energy stores and efficiency in your answer.
model: Moving parts (e.g. pistons and cylinder walls) rub against each other.
Friction acts between the surfaces, opposing motion.
Work is done against friction.
Energy is transferred to the thermal store of the engine parts, which heat up.
This energy is dissipated to the surroundings and is wasted.
Oil forms a layer between the surfaces, keeping them apart.
This reduces friction, so less energy is transferred to the thermal store.
A greater proportion of the input energy is transferred usefully, so efficiency increases (and less wear / overheating).
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a full logical chain: cause, transfer, waste, how lubricant works, effect on efficiency.

worked.q: A machine is supplied with 2000 J. Before lubrication it wastes 800 J by heating. After lubrication it wastes 300 J. Calculate the efficiency before and after.
steps: Useful energy before = 2000 - 800 = 1200 J.
Efficiency before = 1200 / 2000 = 0.60 (60%).
Useful energy after = 2000 - 300 = 1700 J.
Efficiency after = 1700 / 2000 = 0.85 (85%).
worked.ans: Efficiency rises from 0.60 (60%) to 0.85 (85%) because less energy is wasted by friction.

worked.q: A friction force of 40 N acts on a sliding part that moves 3.0 m. Oiling reduces the friction to 15 N. Calculate the reduction in energy wasted over the same distance.
steps: Work done against friction = force x distance.
Before: 40 x 3.0 = 120 J.
After: 15 x 3.0 = 45 J.
Reduction = 120 - 45 = 75 J.
worked.ans: 75 J less energy is transferred to the thermal store.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a squeaky door hinge becomes quieter and easier to open after it is oiled.
steps: The metal surfaces of the hinge rub together, causing friction.
Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal store and to sound (the squeak), which is wasted.
Oil forms a layer between the surfaces, keeping them apart and reducing friction.
Less force is needed to open the door and less energy is wasted as sound and heating.
worked.ans: Oil reduces friction, so less energy is wasted, the squeak stops and less effort is needed.
